info.name: Solvia — PayPal sandbox flow (the app's own API) — REDO
info.description: Tests Solvia's OWN API surface — the exact calls the Solvia checkout page makes. The app itself talks to the PayPal sandbox server-side (create order -> buyer approves on sandbox.paypal.com -> capture); this collection drives and asserts the app's side of that flow, against the REDO endpoints: POST /api/paypal/orders, POST /api/paypal/capture, GET /api/verify, POST /api/chat/extract, in that order, preceded by one setup request that fetches the antiforgery token the two PayPal endpoints require (they are [ValidateAntiForgeryToken] in the redo; the token is scraped from the checkout page the same way the page's own script reads it). Honest shapes only: without sandbox keys configured, create-order answers the app's real 503 'not configured' body, capture stops at 400/404 before PayPal is ever called, and the test scripts assert those shapes too. See postman/README.md for import + run steps.

request.description: SETUP, not a flow step. The redo's two PayPal endpoints are antiforgery-protected: the request must carry the header 'RequestVerificationToken: <token>' AND the antiforgery cookie from the SAME page load. This is exactly how the app's own checkout page does it — its script reads the hidden __RequestVerificationToken input inside its #plain-pay-form and sends it as that header, while the browser sends the cookie automatically. Here, this request loads that same checkout page: Postman's cookie jar keeps the cookie, and this request's test script saves the token into the antiforgeryToken environment variable for requests 1 and 2. Leave Postman's cookie jar ON and run the requests in order. The page only renders for an unpaid application with a price above $0 — a paid or $0 permit redirects to My Permits and there is no token to take (use a fresh, unpaid permitApplicationId).

request.description: Creates the PayPal sandbox order for one permit application (REDO route: /api/paypal/orders — the frozen v1 route was /api/paypal/create-order). The amount is NEVER in this request — the server takes it from the application's snapshotted PriceCents (the college's real fees.csv fee). Run request 0 first: this call needs its antiforgery token header + cookie. Set the permitApplicationId variable first (see README). Success is { "id": "<order id>", "status": "created" } and the test script saves the order id into the paypalOrderId environment variable for request 2. An application that needs no payment answers { "id": null, "status": "not-required" } with no PayPal call at all (Employee exemption, a genuinely $0 permit, is settled this way); an already-Paid one answers status "already-paid". An unknown id answers 404 { "error": "That permit application was not found." } and another demo person's answers 403 — both before PayPal is consulted.

request.description:
Captures an approved sandbox order. Run requests 0 and 1 first — request 1 stores the new order id in the paypalOrderId environment variable, and this call needs request 0's antiforgery token header + cookie.

*** THE HUMAN STEP THIS COLLECTION CANNOT DO FOR YOU ***
Between create (request 1) and capture (this request), a person must approve the order on sandbox.paypal.com: in the app that is the browser checkout flow (the PayPal buttons, or the plain redirect), signed in with a sandbox BUYER account (developer.paypal.com -> Sandbox -> Accounts), clicking Approve/Pay. No API call, Postman included, can approve an order — approval is the buyer's click on PayPal's own page. Capturing an order nobody approved does NOT mark anything paid: PayPal refuses it and Solvia answers 502 { "error": "PayPal sandbox could not capture the order. The permit is not paid." } (or, if PayPal returns a non-COMPLETED status, 200 with completed: false). Paid is set only from a COMPLETED capture, server-side.

Without sandbox keys there is no order to capture at all: request 1 answered 503, paypalOrderId is empty, and this request honestly stops at 400 { "error": "An order id is required." }; with an order id no application owns it stops at 404.

request.description: Public permit verification, JSON door (the redo's VerifyApiController): the same VerifyViewModel the /verify page renders, serialized — same fields, same verdict, nothing extra. Anonymous on purpose: the unguessable token issued when the permit went live is the credential. No antiforgery token is needed (it is a GET). Set the verifyToken variable from the verify link printed on the receipt page after a payment or free issue. An unknown or empty token still answers a calm 200 with found: false and every permit field null — never a 500 and never a hint about other permits. The plate itself is never in the answer (plateState only), and no student name or email ever rides along. A shared 60-requests-per-minute per-IP limit guards this door; past it the answer is 429 { "error": ... }.

request.description: The endpoint the student flow calls per message. No antiforgery token: this JSON endpoint is not antiforgery-protected (only the two PayPal endpoints are). The local model (Microsoft Phi-4-mini via Ollama) answers when it is up; the deterministic fallback answers otherwise — the demo never dies either way, and 'source' says which one answered. The draft carries no price, ever.
